questions.prompt: Complete: "Nobody moved: the teacher was giving ___ to the boy who had fallen in the yard."
questions.explanation: English has fixed first aid as the name of the help given on the spot before a doctor arrives — first help, first care and first cure are all built from perfectly correct words and none of them exists. That is what a collocation is: a partnership usage has already chosen for you, with no rule behind it, which is why the only reliable test is whether you have met the phrase in real English.

questions.prompt: This sentence comes from an American newspaper: "The driver of the lorry paid the check and drove back to his apartment." One word does not belong to the variety the text is written in. Which one?
questions.explanation: Check and apartment are the American words for what the British call a bill and a flat, and driver belongs to both varieties — but lorry is the British word for what Americans call a truck. Neither variety is more correct than the other; the rule is consistency: once a text starts in American English it stays there from beginning to end, so a British lorry never parks in an American paragraph.

questions.prompt: "After many disagreements, the two families decided to put aside their differences." Here, to put aside means to…
questions.explanation: Put aside carries several meanings, and the words that follow it decide which one applies: with money it means to save (put aside money for a rainy day), with a newspaper it means to lay something down for a moment, and with differences, fears or doubts it means to forget them, to disregard them, to leave them behind. Reading it as saving something for later takes the money sense into a sentence that does not fit it. This is why a dictionary of synonyms lists a phrasal verb example by example instead of once and for all — and why you read the whole sentence before you choose a meaning.

questions.prompt: In the bibliography entry "Cherif, N. 2011. Writing for the Exam. Sousse: Dar El Ilm.", which element names the publisher?
questions.explanation: A bibliography entry always runs in the same order: last name, initial of the first name, date of publication, title of the book, then place and publisher. Dar El Ilm comes last, after the place, so it is the publisher; Sousse is only where it is based. Cherif is the author's last name, 2011 is the date of publication, and Writing for the Exam is the title.

questions.prompt: Complete: "The lawyer opened a window to let in some fresh ___, and then read out the name of the only ___."
questions.explanation: Air is what you breathe and an heir is the person who will inherit; the h of heir is silent, so the two are pronounced exactly alike and are homophones. Nothing in the sound tells you which spelling to write, and only the words around each gap can: a window is opened for fresh air, and a fortune is read out to an heir. No spellchecker will ever flag the mistake either, because both spellings are real English words.

questions.prompt: Sonia grew up speaking Arabic with her family and French at school. Which word describes her?
questions.explanation: The prefix bi- means two, so a speaker of two languages is bilingual. Mono- means one, and a monolingual speaker has only one language; multi- means many, so multilingual describes somebody who handles several. The same prefixes are at work on the word culture — bicultural, multicultural — which is why reading the prefix is very often enough to read the whole word.
